messages.author: 97d82fedb7016adb
messages.subject: unused parameters
parts:
Hi!

I was wondering how badly the sampler performance is affected if I have an extra parameter in my Stan model which is not associated to data at all (which can happen for some subsets of my data).

Is that very bad news in terms of performance or is everything fine as long as I put a normal(0,1) on it?

Best,
Sebastian

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] unused parameters
parts:
Stan does the right thing --- the posterior will just be equal to
the prior. If the prior's normal(0,1), it shouldn't be too much
of a burden computationally.

- Bob

messages.author: f53f4ca2c430170d
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] unused parameters
parts:
On Friday, April 17, 2015 at 10:19:04 AM UTC-4, Sebastian Weber wrote:
My concern was not with the free parameter, but rather with the sampling efficiency of NUTS with respect to all other parameters. I am asking, because I burned myself once with a model where I forgot to put a prior on some parameter which did not end up in the likelihood for some reasons... this killed NUTS; but I take that as long as a sensible prior is in place all is good.

Right, that makes sense since then the posterior is improper and that one parameter would not meet the conditions for a U-turn... I recall there's some parameter that limits the maximum number of steps but not what it's called.  If the prior is normal(0,sigma) (i.e. the parameter is an unused random effect level) you could get the funnel posterior and have a similar problem, but only if sigma is estimated to be large...  and that's where my intuition for this runs out.

Krzysztof

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] unused parameters
parts:
> On Apr 18, 2015, at 12:39 AM, Krzysztof Sakrejda <krzysztof...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> On Friday, April 17, 2015 at 10:19:04 AM UTC-4, Sebastian Weber wrote:
> My concern was not with the free parameter, but rather with the sampling efficiency of NUTS with respect to all other parameters. I am asking, because I burned myself once with a model where I forgot to put a prior on some parameter which did not end up in the likelihood for some reasons... this killed NUTS; but I take that as long as a sensible prior is in place all is good.
>
> Right, that makes sense since then the posterior is improper and that one parameter would not meet the conditions for a U-turn...

The posterior has to be proper or NUTS will run with the
impropriety.

I just meant in my response that an extra normal(0,1) variable
will absolutely not kill the NUTS condition and not slow things
down overall very much.
> I recall there's some parameter that limits the maximum number of steps but not what it's called.

That just masks the problem. Whenver you bump up against the limit, either
the model needs to be fixed or the limit needs to be extended. It's there
so Stan doesn't just hang on the first go-round.

> If the prior is normal(0,sigma) (i.e. the parameter is an unused random effect level) you could get the funnel posterior and have a similar problem, but only if sigma is estimated to be large... and that's where my intuition for this runs out.

This isn't relevant if you have a fixed normal(0,1) prior,
or even if it's a hierarchical prior that's well constrained.

The problem with the funnel is the curvature issue --- with
high hyperprior variance, the posterior is flat, whereas with
low hyperprior variance, the posterior is very sharply curved.
So you can't get a mass matrix and step-size that work everywhere.

The manual covers both these cases in the problematic posterior
and reparameterization chapters.

- Bob

messages.author: f53f4ca2c430170d
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] unused parameters
parts: On Friday, April 17, 2015 at 10:51:03 AM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:

> On Apr 18, 2015, at 12:39 AM, Krzysztof Sakrejda <krzysztof...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> On Friday, April 17, 2015 at 10:19:04 AM UTC-4, Sebastian Weber wrote:
[snip]

The posterior has to be proper or NUTS will run with the
impropriety.  

I just meant in my response that an extra normal(0,1) variable
will absolutely not kill the NUTS condition and not slow things
down overall very much.
I was not disagreeing, sorry if that wasn't clear.

> I recall there's some parameter that limits the maximum number of steps but not what it's called.

That just masks the problem.  Whenver you bump up against the limit, either
the model needs to be fixed or the limit needs to be extended.  It's there
so Stan doesn't just hang on the first go-round.

>  If the prior is normal(0,sigma) (i.e. the parameter is an unused random effect level) you could get the funnel posterior and have a similar problem, but only if sigma is estimated to be large...  and that's where my intuition for this runs out.

This isn't relevant if you have a fixed normal(0,1) prior,
or even if it's a hierarchical prior that's well constrained.

The problem with the funnel is the curvature issue --- with
high hyperprior variance, the posterior is flat, whereas with
low hyperprior variance, the posterior is very sharply curved.
So you can't get a mass matrix and step-size that work everywhere.

I was just coming up with other situations where you could loose efficiency and if you have a hierarchical model where sigma is large (e.g.-outliers, but mostly well-estimated) then an unused random effect would have the funnel posterior and if the mass matrix gets estimated wrong (small step size) then it would kill performance when sigma got large at later iterations.  I've had this happen for a mark-recapture model with per-occasion random effects for recapture, so I think it's worth being careful with weeding out parameters for batches with no/little data in a hierarchical model. 

Krzysztof

The manual covers both these cases in the problematic posterior
and reparameterization chapters.

- Bob

By well constrained, I meant the hierarchical parameters, so that
you really get the effect of sampling from a fixed normal.

Which brings us to your next paragraph :-)

> I was just coming up with other situations where you could loose efficiency and if you have a hierarchical model where sigma is large (e.g.-outliers, but mostly well-estimated) then an unused random effect would have the funnel posterior and if the mass matrix gets estimated wrong (small step size) then it would kill performance when sigma got large at later iterations. I've had this happen for a mark-recapture model with per-occasion random effects for recapture, so I think it's worth being careful with weeding out parameters for batches with no/little data in a hierarchical model.

Absolutely. That's one of the reasons we've been going toward
stronger priors and hyperpriors.

And if at all possible, unused parameters should be removed. It
just makes everything less efficient.

- Bob
